articles.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers
articles.excerpt: Our new repo star history API now provides trends without returning individual identities or requiring unbounded database work. These are the engineering tradeoffs we made. The post From 2,500 request…
articles.body: Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away. Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page. The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people.

articles.body: Excluding Cross‑Property Devices from Metrics and Adding Live Scan Tracking in monitor‑parches‑uhpcm TL;DR: I refactored the analysis layer to drop equipment belonging to other properties (AHCUN, BKCUN, …) and exposed a live “scan launched” flag in the UI. The change removes noisy data from the dashboards and gives operators instant feedback when a scan is triggered from Endpoint Central. The Problem Our internal patch‑monitoring dashboard aggregates device data from several physical locations (Playa, AHCUN, BKCUN, KKCUN, HRPUJ, …). The metrics view ( /metrics ) displayed totals for all devices, even though the user had selected a single property. The result was inflated “missing patches” counts and misleading charts.

articles.title: My short link click-stats API taught me that 'last click time' is a lie you tell yourself
articles.excerpt: Built a click-analytics endpoint for the short links my agents create. Total clicks, clicks in the last 30 days, last click timestamp. Simple counters, increment on redirect, store in a map, read back…
articles.body: Built a click-analytics endpoint for the short links my agents create. Total clicks, clicks in the last 30 days, last click timestamp. Simple counters, increment on redirect, store in a map, read back with the manage secret. Shipped it, watched the dashboard fill up. Then an agent asked a reasonable question: "Which of my 40 links is dying?" I couldn't answer. Because I had total clicks and last click time , but no time series. A link with 900 clicks, all in January, and a link with 900 clicks spread across six months look identical in my stats. One is dead. One is alive. My API can't tell them apart. The fix wasn't glamorous. I added a ring buffer of the last 30 days, one counter per day, rotated lazily on read. No time-series database, no Prometheus, no infra.

articles.title: My FastAPI Dependency Ran Once When I Needed It Twice
articles.excerpt: I had a FastAPI endpoint that needed two different rate-limit checks: one against the user's account, one against their IP. I wrote a clean little dependency to do a check, declared it twice with diff…
articles.body: I had a FastAPI endpoint that needed two different rate-limit checks: one against the user's account, one against their IP. I wrote a clean little dependency to do a check, declared it twice with different arguments, and shipped it. It passed review. It worked in testing. And in production, one of the two checks just… wasn't happening. Users who should have been blocked by the IP limit were sailing through. The account check fired; the IP check behaved as if it had already run and returned the same answer. I added logging. The dependency function was being called once. I declared it twice. It ran once. I stared at that for a long time. "I literally wrote Depends() twice.

articles.title: Researchers Hid a Mailbox in Offscreen Text. AI Agents Sent It 33 Messages
articles.excerpt: Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews The series: Pocket Guides for Developers — 8 short books on agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design — the whole series My…

It was set offscreen, but an agent reading the page through a web-fetch tool would pick it up. The text pointed to a mailbox, and agents sent 33 messages to it across 13 threads . articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.

articles.title: Life after the moon: Artemis II's Christina Koch steps down from active astronaut duty
articles.excerpt: Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become NASA's acting deputy chief engineer on Nov. 1. All four Artemis II crewmates have now stepped away from active spaceflight duties.
articles.body: Don't expect any of the Artemis II moon astronauts to fly again soon. On Tuesday (Oct. 13), NASA announced that Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. "With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments," NASA officials wrote in a statement on Tuesday . Her three Artemis II crewmates had already shared their next moves, none of which put another spaceflight in play in the near future. Mission commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover , both of NASA, became "emeritus" astronauts last month, a role that seems to include planning, advising and mentoring duties but no flights into the final frontier.
articles.author: Mike Wall

articles.title: NASA’s Space X CRS-35 Launch Jellyfish
articles.excerpt: Sunlight illuminates the exhaust plumes of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft on Oct. 13, 2026. This visual phenomenon is known as a “jellyfish”; it happens near sunrise…
articles.body: NASA/John Kraus Sunlight illuminates the exhaust plumes of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft on Oct. 13, 2026. This visual phenomenon is known as a “jellyfish”; it happens near sunrise or sunset when the exhaust plume from the rocket becomes brightly illuminated, creating a glowing shape resembling a jellyfish. The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, carrying scientific investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station on SpaceX’s 35th commercial resupply services mission for NASA. The rocket’s exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States.

articles.title: 'The X-Files' is officially returning as Hulu picks up Ryan Coogler's 'reimagining' of the sci-fi icon
articles.excerpt: Trust no one.
articles.body: The truth is once again out there, as Disney & Hulu confirmed today that they have picked up a new "The X-Files" show for a full season. Described as a "reimagining" of the classic series, the project comes from Ryan Coogler, the acclaimed writer and director of "Creed", "Black Panther", and "Sinners", and will star Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel. The show's premise will sound very familiar to fans of the original, as it centers on "two highly decorated but vastly different FBI agents who form an unlikely bond when they are assigned to a long-shuttered division devoted to cases involving unexplained phenomena." "I've loved 'The X-Files' for a long time, so getting the chance to write and direct the pilot has meant a great deal to me," said Coogler.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
